# Corn

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="corn-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="corn-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="corn-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Monitored maize grain and sweet corn are mostly below reporting limits for lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury; corn grown downwind of industry, beside power plants, on wastewater-irrigated fields or in mining areas carried several times more.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Lead and cadmium in maize grain from contaminated fields; arsenic where soil or water is high in it; mercury near coal-fired power plants.<sup </li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Where the corn grew, irrigation water, the form bought (dry grain or sweet corn) and the basis a result is reported on.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S. El-Hassanin, Magdy R. Samak, Gomaa N. Abdel-Rahman, Yahia H. Abu-Sree, Essam M. Saleh · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Risk assessment of human exposure to lead and cadmium in maize grains cultivated in soils irrigated either with low-quality water or freshwater</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 7:10-15</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Gu Q, Yu T, Yang Z, Ji J, Hou Q, Wang L, Wei X, Zhang Q · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Prediction and risk assessment of five heavy metals in maize and peanut: a case study of Guangxi, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Toxicology and Pharmacology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<li>

<a id="overview"></a>
<a id="decision-summary"></a>
## Corn overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>
<a id="which-sourcing-or-production-decisions-deserve-priority-on-the-available-evidence"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-006"></a>
<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

Most corn sold as maize grain or sweet corn carries lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury below or near the limits laboratories can measure. In WHO GEMS/Food, European maize grain had a median lead result below 20 µg/kg across 890 results from 2001 to 2020, and 8 exceeded the EU and Codex cereal limit of 200 µg/kg; cadmium had a median below 3.2 µg/kg, with 3 of 1,238 results above the 100 µg/kg limit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/codex-cxs-193-1995|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Codex Alimentarius Commission · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Codex Alimentarius (Joint FAO/WHO Food Standards Programme)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Frozen corn boiled as eaten in the US Total Diet Study had lead, arsenic and mercury below detection in all 27 national composites, and a median cadmium of 2.6 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

The exceptions come from where the corn grew. Maize from farms downwind of a Nigerian cement plant averaged 230–380 µg/kg lead against 20 µg/kg at a control farm, maize irrigated with wastewater in Egypt carried 260–550 µg/kg lead against 30–40 µg/kg or less with fresh or ground water, and maize within 1 km of Chinese coal-fired power plants held about 21 µg/kg mercury against about 1 µg/kg at 5 km and 0.72 µg/kg in maize from a distant grocery store.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S. El-Hassanin, Magdy R. Samak, Gomaa N. Abdel-Rahman, Yahia H. Abu-Sree, Essam M. Saleh · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Risk assessment of human exposure to lead and cadmium in maize grains cultivated in soils irrigated either with low-quality water or freshwater</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 7:10-15</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span Compaore MKA, Bande M, Kpoda SD, Meda NSBR, Ouedraogo Kangambega TM, Ilboudo I, Sandwidi BY, Nikiema F, Yakoro A, Bassole IHN, Hien H, Kabre E · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" For a buyer the practical points are the growing area, the form bought and the laboratory’s quantification limit. Maize grain and sweet corn have different legal limits: the EU allows 200 µg/kg lead and 100 µg/kg cadmium in cereals but 100 µg/kg lead and 20 µg/kg cadmium in sweet corn, on a wet-weight basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Lot results with a quantification limit well below those values are the supported check; testing finds contamination but does not remove it.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>



<a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## What counts as corn

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers corn (Zea mays) in two forms that are measured and regulated differently: mature maize grain, the dry kernels sold as a cereal, and fresh corn, meaning sweet corn or green ears eaten as a vegetable raw, frozen or cooked, together with baby corn.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-corn" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-corn-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of corn, group and metal. Maize grain, fresh or frozen sweet corn, cooked sweet corn and baby corn are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-field medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a polluted site with its control, one season with another, or cooked with raw sweet corn. Held rows failed a check against their own paper and are shown but not compared.</p>

data-shared-occurrence-methods><summary>Shared dataset methods and interpretation</summary><div data-shared-evidence-content><p>Source summaries retain their original statistic, material, basis and censoring. Each source drawer identifies methods and overlapping samples. No matched reference or pooled distribution is inferred.</p></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:corn-grain-fw-Pb:a59995895459"><summary>HMI corn Pb reference · Maize grain</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:corn-grain-fw-Pb:a59995895459"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI corn Pb reference · Maize grain. Maize grain; As sold, as eaten or fresh weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>≤15</td><td>≤26.4</td><td>13–50 (bounded)</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>≤15</td><td>≤26.4</td><td>13–50 (bounded)</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>37 reference units; 1 sampling family. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>37</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for maize grain on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: individual WHO GEMS/Food results summarized as one median per WHO region, sampling type and collection year. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms of corn, other bases, results without a stated basis and grain from mining-, industry- or wastewater-affected fields are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>GEMS/Food is the only compatible sampling family for maize grain on this basis in the completed corn ledger, so this single-family reference cannot represent other markets. WHO regions are reporting regions, not growing areas. Many results are non-detects with differing limits, which widens the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. Method: hmi-pooled-reference-v2.</p><p>hmi-pooled-reference-v2:corn-grain-fw-Pb:a59995895459</p><p>The reference is computed by HMI from admitted evidence, not copied from a study baseline. It describes the evidence currently in this scope; it is not a worldwide or current-lot benchmark. Source, year and region filters do not change it. Different HMI scopes are not one common ranking.</p></details></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:corn-grain-dw-Pb:28587d1e6c2a"><summary>HMI corn Pb reference · Maize grain, dry weight</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:corn-grain-dw-Pb:28587d1e6c2a"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI corn Pb reference · Maize grain, dry weight. Maize grain; Dry weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>≤1</td><td>10–10.5 (bounded)</td><td>20</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>≤1</td><td>10–10.5 (bounded)</td><td>20</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>2 reference units; 2 sampling families. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>1</td><td>50%</td></tr><tr><td>Abatemi-Usman et al. 2023</td><td>1</td><td>50%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for maize grain on a dry weight basis: individual WHO GEMS/Food results summarized as one median per WHO region, sampling type and collection year, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary fields or markets in the literature. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms of corn, other bases, results without a stated basis and grain from mining-, industry- or wastewater-affected fields are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach corn

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

Corn takes up cadmium and nickel from soil into the grain, while lead and mercury reach the grain more from air and dust deposited on the plant.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Gu Q, Yu T, Yang Z, Ji J, Hou Q, Wang L, Wei X, Zhang Q · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Prediction and risk assessment of five heavy metals in maize and peanut: a case study of Guangxi, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Toxicology and Pharmacology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Guangxi, maize grain cadmium and lead uptake fell as soil organic carbon and manganese rose, and cadmium uptake also fell with higher soil pH, across 65 paired grain and soil samples.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Gu Q, Yu T, Yang Z, Ji J, Hou Q, Wang L, Wei X, Zhang Q · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Prediction and risk assessment of five heavy metals in maize and peanut: a case study of Guangxi, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Toxicology and Pharmacology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Bangladesh, soil-to-grain transfer factors for maize were 0.054 for cadmium and 0.014 for lead, so grain carried a small fraction of soil levels.<sup class="cite">[[sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Islam MS, Ahmed MK, Habibullah-Al-Mamun M · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals">Heavy Metals in Cereals and Pulses: Health Implications in Bangladesh</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Industrial emissions raise the metals in corn grown nearby. At five farms around a cement plant at Obajana, Kogi State, Nigeria, maize harvested in 2017 averaged 230–380 µg/kg lead on a dry-weight basis at the three downwind farms against 20 µg/kg at a control farm 18 km upwind.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Near two Chinese coal-fired power plants, maize mercury fell from about 21 µg/kg at 1 km to 4.7–6.7 µg/kg at 3 km and 1.06 µg/kg at 5 km, on a fresh-weight basis, against 0.72 µg/kg in maize from a grocery store more than 55 km away.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Maize from a village 2.5 km from a battery plant in Henan averaged 140 µg/kg lead and 70 µg/kg mercury, with the basis not stated.<sup class="cite">[[sources/jiang2020-henan-battery-factory-crops-metals|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Jiang Y, Ma J, Ruan X · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/jiang2020-henan-battery-factory-crops-metals">Compound health risk assessment of cumulative heavy metal exposure: A case study of a village near a battery factory in Henan Province, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Science: Processes &amp; Impacts</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/jiang2020-henan-battery-factory-crops-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Irrigation water and mining waste are the other routes in the evidence. In Egypt, maize irrigated with sewage or industrial wastewater carried 260–550 µg/kg lead and 38–112 µg/kg cadmium, against 30–40 µg/kg lead and 9–10 µg/kg cadmium or less with Nile or ground water, basis not stated.<sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S. El-Hassanin, Magdy R. Samak, Gomaa N. Abdel-Rahman, Yahia H. Abu-Sree, Essam M. Saleh · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Risk assessment of human exposure to lead and cadmium in maize grains cultivated in soils irrigated either with low-quality water or freshwater</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 7:10-15</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In a high-arsenic coal-burning area of Shaanxi, China, corn dried before analysis held 4,240 µg/kg arsenic, and a corn sample from a gold-mining orchard in Ecuador held 740 µg/kg arsenic and 1,620 µg/kg nickel.<sup class="cite">[[sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining|14]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Romero-Crespo P, Jiménez-Oyola S, Salgado-Almeida B, Zambrano-Anchundia J, Goyburo-Chávez C, González-Valoys A, Higueras class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bai AM, Li Q, Li Y, Fan ZX, Li XQ, Tan WH, Cao DY, Kang YJ · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-living-near-a-factory-or-power-plant-affect-corn-grown-there" data-anchor="does-living-near-a-factory-or-power-plant-affect-corn-grown-there" data-question="Does living near a factory or power plant affect corn grown there?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does living near a factory or power plant affect corn grown there?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, yes: maize downwind of a cement plant averaged 230–380 µg/kg lead against 20 µg/kg at a control farm, and maize within 1 km of coal-fired power plants held about 21 µg/kg mercury against about 1 µg/kg at 5 km.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> These are single observational studies, so the size of the effect elsewhere depends on emissions, wind and distance.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<a id="ranges-by-source-region-and-variety"></a>
## Which forms and regions measured lower

<a id="hmi-ing-013"></a>
<a id="how-do-concentrations-vary-by-origin-growing-conditions-variety-and-harvest-period"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-014"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-distinguishes-within-lot-between-lot-supplier-and-production-system-variation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-015"></a>
<a id="which-comparisons-support-a-sourcing-decision-and-where-would-geographic-or-supplier-generalization-be-unjustified"></a>

For lead, fresh and cooked sweet corn measured lowest in the evidence. Frozen corn boiled as eaten had lead below 4 µg/kg in all 27 US Total Diet Study composites from 2017 to 2020, and only 1 of 65 cooked sweet corn results submitted to GEMS/Food from the Americas in 2000–2017 was detected.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Raw sweet corn had median lead below 10 µg/kg in European and South-East Asian submissions and below 1.4 µg/kg in 65 results from the Americas in 2014–2016, while maize grain had a median below 20 µg/kg in Europe.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Sweet corn is mostly water, so these per-kilogram differences do not show that sweet corn plants take up less lead than grain maize.

Among regions reporting maize grain, European results were lowest for lead and Western Pacific results highest.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Western Pacific submissions from 2001 to 2010, almost all labelled domestic, had a median of 29–50 µg/kg and 24 of 327 above 200 µg/kg, against 8 of 890 in Europe.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Within Europe, maize labelled imported had a median below 17 µg/kg and a highest detected value of 155 µg/kg, against a median below 20 µg/kg and a highest value of 790 µg/kg for domestic maize, a tentative difference from 48 imported results.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> WHO regions are reporting regions, not growing areas, so this does not identify producing countries with lower lead.

European maize lead also fell over time.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> 4 of 233 grain results from 2001–2007 and 4 of 257 from 2008–2013 exceeded 200 µg/kg, against none of 400 from 2014–2020.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For cadmium, monitored maize grain and sweet corn were both low, and imported sweet corn measured lower than domestic sweet corn in Europe.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span →</a></span></span></sup> European grain had a median below 3.2 µg/kg, and European sweet corn a median of 1–4 µg/kg; sweet corn labelled imported had a median below 2.4 µg/kg against 2.6–4 µg/kg for domestic, from 138 and 129 results.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Maize from Bangladesh fields averaged 640 µg/kg total arsenic on a dry-weight basis, and Sri Lankan farm maize averaged 91 µg/kg wet weight with most results below detection, so arsenic depends strongly on local soil and water.<sup class="cite">[[sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Islam MS, Ahmed MK, Habibullah-Al-Mamun M · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals">Heavy Metals in Cereals and Pulses: Health Implications in Bangladesh</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/edirisinghe2019-sri-lanka-legumes-cereals-as-cd|19]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Edirisinghe EMRKB, Jinadasa BKKK · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/edirisinghe2019-sri-lanka-legumes-cereals-as-cd">Arsenic and cadmium concentrations in legumes and cereals grown in the North Central Province, Sri Lanka and assessment of their health risk</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Contamination 6:3</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/edirisinghe2019-sri-lanka-legumes-cereals-as-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="is-sweet-corn-lower-in-heavy-metals-than-maize-grain" data-anchor="is-sweet-corn-lower-in-heavy-metals-than-maize-grain" data-question="Is sweet corn lower in heavy metals than maize grain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Is sweet corn lower in heavy metals than maize grain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Per kilogram, yes, for lead in the monitoring evidence: raw sweet corn medians were below 1.4–10 µg/kg and cooked US sweet corn was below 4 µg/kg in every composite, against a European grain median below 20 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Sweet corn is mostly water and grain is dry, so this reflects the food as eaten rather than lower uptake, and the EU sets a lower lead limit for sweet corn (100 µg/kg) than for cereals (200 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-reported-the-lowest-lead-in-maize-grain" data-anchor="which-regions-reported-the-lowest-lead-in-maize-grain" data-question="Which regions reported the lowest lead in maize grain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions reported the lowest lead in maize grain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

European submissions, with a median below 20 µg/kg and 8 of 890 results above 200 µg/kg, against 24 of 327 above 200 µg/kg in Western Pacific submissions from 2001–2010.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> These are reporting markets, mostly of domestic grain, so they show where testing found lower lead rather than which countries grow cleaner maize.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>


<a id="processing-effects"></a>
<a id="ingredient-derivative-risk"></a>
<a id="processing-effects-and-derivatives"></a>
## Drying, cooking and processing

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

No study in the library measured the same corn before and after washing, husking, milling, soaking or cooking for metals. Cooking was compared only across different samples: cooked sweet corn submitted to GEMS/Food had lead and cadmium medians similar to raw sweet corn from the same region, with overlapping reporting limits.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Heat does not destroy metals, so cooking can lower a concentration only by moving metal into water or adding water to the food.

Drying works the other way. Field studies report dried grain, and drying raises the concentration per kilogram because water is removed, so dry-weight results cannot be set against sweet corn as eaten.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/saleem2025-nd-vegetables-hra|15]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Saleem M, Wang Y, Pierce D, Sens DA, Somji S, Garrett SH · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/saleem2025-nd-vegetables-hra">Concentration and Potential Non-Carcinogenic and Carcinogenic Health Risk Assessment of Metals in Locally Grown Vegetables</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/saleem2025-nd-vegetables-hra">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2022-guizhou-cd-grains|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li X, Zhou L, Zhang C, Li D, Wang Z, Sun D, Liao C, Zhang Q · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2022-guizhou-cd-grains">Spatial distribution and risk assessment of fluorine and cadmium in rice, corn, and wheat grains in most karst regions of Guizhou province, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Nutrition</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2022-guizhou-cd-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Fresh sweet corn from a North Dakota farmers’ market, measured after oven drying, had 7 µg/kg lead and 6 µg/kg cadmium on a dry-weight basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/saleem2025-nd-vegetables-hra|15]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Saleem M, Wang Y, Pierce D, Sens DA, Somji S, Garrett SH · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/saleem2025-nd-vegetables-hra">Concentration and Potential Non-Carcinogenic and Carcinogenic Health Risk Assessment of Metals in Locally Grown Vegetables</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/saleem2025-nd-vegetables-hra">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Milled and processed maize foods are outside this page, but one comparison shows why corn matters to their contamination. European infant porridges and cakes that mixed rice with maize and other grains had median inorganic arsenic of 10 and 8 µg/kg against 66 and 60 µg/kg for pure rice products, although maize’s own contribution was not separated.<sup class="cite">[[sources/carey2018-rice-dilution-infant-food-eu-arsenic|28]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Carey M, Donaldson E, Signes-Pastor AJ, Meharg AA · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/carey2018-rice-dilution-infant-food-eu-arsenic">Dilution of rice with other gluten free grains to lower inorganic arsenic in foods for young children in response to European Union regulations provides impetus to setting stricter standards</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">PLoS ONE</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/carey2018-rice-dilution-infant-food-eu-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>



<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Mitigation from field to lot

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Measured or observed controls for metals in corn act at the field and at lot release. Field siting has the clearest evidence: grain from farms downwind of a cement plant, irrigated with wastewater, or within 3 km of coal-fired power plants carried several to many times more lead or mercury than grain from control sites in the same studies.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S. El-Hassanin, Magdy R. Samak, Gomaa N. Abdel-Rahman, Yahia H. Abu-Sree, Essam M. Saleh · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Risk assessment of human exposure to lead and cadmium in maize grains cultivated in soils irrigated either with low-quality water or freshwater</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 7:10-15</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> These are observational comparisons, not tested interventions, and they come from single studies in Nigeria, Egypt and China.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S. El-Hassanin, Magdy R. Samak, Gomaa N. Abdel-Rahman, Yahia H. Abu-Sree, Essam M. Saleh · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Risk assessment of human exposure to lead and cadmium in maize grains cultivated in soils irrigated either with low-quality water or freshwater</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 7:10-15</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Crop choice changes exposure on contaminated land. Near the Chinese power plants, maize held about a third of the mercury of rice at the same locations (21 against 63 µg/kg at 1 km), and in the Chengdu industrial area maize averaged 260 µg/kg cadmium against 460 µg/kg for rice.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/liu2022-heavy-metals-rice-maize-chengdu|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Liu Q, Li X, He L · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/liu2022-heavy-metals-rice-maize-chengdu">Health risk assessment of heavy metals in soils and food crops from a coexist area of heavily industrialized and intensively cropping in the Chengdu Plain, Sichuan, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/liu2022-heavy-metals-rice-maize-chengdu">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Guangxi, soils richer in organic carbon and manganese, and with higher pH, gave lower cadmium uptake into maize grain, which supports liming and organic amendments as plausible levers, although no amendment was tested on maize grain in the library.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Gu Q, Yu T, Yang Z, Ji J, Hou Q, Wang L, Wei X, Zhang Q · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Prediction and risk assessment of five heavy metals in maize and peanut: a case study of Guangxi, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Toxicology and Pharmacology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gu2019-maize-peanut-heavy-metals-guangxi">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

At release, the supported control is lot testing against the destination limit with an adequate method.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/codex-cxs-193-1995|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Codex Alimentarius Commission · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Codex Alimentarius (Joint FAO/WHO Food Standards Programme)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/codex-cxs-193-1995">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A portable screening method recovered 95–110% of cadmium and lead added to corn, which supports rapid screening, while laboratory confirmation remains necessary.<sup class="cite">[[sources/tian2021-magnetic-purification-cadmium-lead-grain|29]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Tian W, Zhou M, Liu Y, Wu Y, Zhang J, Chen X, Wang S · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/tian2021-magnetic-purification-cadmium-lead-grain">A rapid magnetic-based purification of Cd2+ and Pb2+ prior to portable electrochemical determination for grain</a></span><span A range spanning bands retains both labels; a qualitative label has no implied percentage.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Control in context</p><p>Infant porridges and cakes mixing rice with maize and other gluten-free grains had median inorganic arsenic of 10 and 8 µg/kg, against 66 and 60 µg/kg for pure rice products; maize’s own share was not measured.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Context</th><th scope="col">Selected control</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Material</td><td>Infant porridges and cakes sold in Europe</td></tr><tr><td>Stage</td><td>product formulation</td></tr><tr><td>Audience</td><td>Ingredient suppliers · Brands</td></tr><tr><td>Period</td><td>As reported</td></tr><tr><td>Conditions</td><td>Infant food formulation; maize contribution not isolated.</td></tr><tr><td>Tested scale</td><td>Market survey</td></tr><tr><td>Sample units</td><td>Source sampling units; no independent intervention units unless stated.</td></tr><tr><td>Trade-offs</td><td>Other metals, yield and cost not quantified unless stated.</td></tr><tr><td>Verification</td><td>Confirm with lot-specific lead and cadmium results on the form sold, using an adequate quantification limit.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Design, applicability and operating conditions</p><p>Observational field survey. Infant food formulation; maize contribution not isolated.</p><p>One study family.</p><p>As reported by the source</p><p>Reduces metal reaching corn, or detects it before release.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Source measurements and linked outcomes</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Analyte</th><th scope="col">Period</th><th scope="col">Effect</th><th scope="col">Converted values</th><th scope="col">Original means (SD)</th><th scope="col">Basis</th><th scope="col">Locator</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Inorganic arsenic (iAs)</td><td>As reported</td><td>Multi-grain porridge lower (observational)</td><td>66 → 10 µg/kg</td><td>Absolute values unextracted</td><td>As sold</td><td>Results</td></tr><tr><td>Inorganic arsenic (iAs)</td><td>As reported</td><td>Multi-grain cakes lower (observational)</td><td>60 → 8 µg/kg</td><td>Absolute values unextracted</td><td>As sold</td><td>Results</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>Observational market comparison.</p><p>Differences are read from the source means or medians shown in outcomes.</p><p>Basis as stated in outcomes; Grain and sweet corn are judged against different limits. A sweet corn lot at 50 µg/kg lead is within the EU sweet corn limit of 100 µg/kg, while the same value in grain would be a quarter of the cereal limit; comparing them per kilogram without moisture mixes two different foods.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<a id="finished-product-and-exposure-implications"></a>
## Exposure from corn

<a id="hmi-ing-031"></a>
<a id="how-do-inclusion-rate-processing-yield-preparation-and-other-ingredients-affect-a-finished-product-estimate"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-032"></a>
<a id="how-do-consumption-patterns-and-intended-populations-affect-dietary-exposure-interpretation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-033"></a>
<a id="what-conclusions-require-finished-product-measurements-or-a-separate-exposure-assessment"></a>

Corn is a staple in Africa and Latin America and a common vegetable elsewhere, so its share of metal intake depends heavily on how much is eaten. No source in the ledger gives a verified population estimate of lead or cadmium intake from maize grain or sweet corn. A Henan village study estimated that adults ate 13.5 g of corn a day, and several field studies report intake indices, but most rest on dry-weight values applied to as-eaten intake or on concentrations held for integrity problems.<sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S. El-Hassanin, Magdy R. Samak, Gomaa N. Abdel-Rahman, Yahia H. Abu-Sree, Essam M. Saleh · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Risk assessment of human exposure to lead and cadmium in maize grains cultivated in soils irrigated either with low-quality water or freshwater</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 7:10-15</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Islam MS, Ahmed MK, Habibullah-Al-Mamun M · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals">Heavy Metals in Cereals and Pulses: Health Implications in Bangladesh</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/islam2014-bangladesh-cereals-pulses-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/jiang2020-henan-battery-factory-crops-metals|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Jiang Y, Ma J, Ruan X · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/jiang2020-henan-battery-factory-crops-metals">Compound health risk assessment of cumulative heavy metal exposure: A case study of a village near a battery factory in Henan Province, China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Science: Processes &amp; Impacts</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/jiang2020-henan-battery-factory-crops-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Monitoring results bound the contribution for typical retail corn. With cooked US sweet corn below 4 µg/kg lead and 1 µg/kg mercury in every composite, and median cadmium of 2.6 µg/kg, ordinary retail sweet corn adds little per serving compared with the limits.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Where maize is eaten daily as a staple, the field results above 200 µg/kg lead in Burkina Faso, Bangladesh and contaminated areas are the cases that would matter for intake, but none was turned into a verified exposure estimate.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S.
